subject: Climate & Environment
title: The Great Ocean Conveyor Belt
description: A fast breakdown of The Great Ocean Conveyor Belt for builders.

hook.text: A single loop of ocean current takes about 1,000 years to circle the globe. It never stops.

buildup.text: Cold, salty water sinks in the North Atlantic and flows along the ocean floor toward Antarctica.

discovery.text: It slowly rises, warms, and flows back on the surface — distributing heat across the planet.

twist.text: This thermohaline circulation drives weather patterns for billions of people.

climax.text: If it slows or stops, Europe could cool dramatically while the tropics overheat.

punchline.text: The slowest current on Earth controls the fastest changes in weather.

quiz.question: How long does it take for water to complete one loop of the conveyor belt?

details.summary: The global thermohaline circulation is a system of deep-ocean currents that moves heat, salt, and nutrients around the planet. Cold, salty water sinks near the poles, flows along the ocean floor, and eventually resurfaces in warmer regions, completing a cycle that takes roughly a thousand years.
details.whyItMatters: This conveyor belt distributes heat from the tropics to higher latitudes and drives nutrient cycling. Its disruption could dramatically alter weather patterns worldwide.
takeaways: Cold salty water sinks near the poles and drives deep currents
The full circulation loop takes about a thousand years
It moves heat poleward and nutrients toward the surface

faq.question: What drives the thermohaline circulation?
faq.answer: Differences in water density caused by temperature and salinity. Near the poles, surface water cools and becomes saltier as sea ice forms, making it dense enough to sink to the ocean floor and push the circulation forward.

faq.question: Could global warming shut down the conveyor belt?
faq.answer: Melting ice sheets add fresh water to polar seas, reducing salinity and making surface water less dense. If enough freshwater enters, sinking could slow or stop, weakening the circulation. Models suggest a slowdown is already underway.
